abstract: Power matters for AI safety. Optimal agents tend to acquire power across a wide range of objectives (instrumental convergence). Concurrently, as we embed AI agents into socio-technical systems, humans risk gradual disempowerment. Both concerns call for a formal, quantitative measure of power. Two such measures in the context of Markov games (multi-agent MDPs) are information-theoretic empowerment, the capacity of the channel from an agent’s actions to future states, and capability-based individual power, a measure of goal attainment built from the probabilities that a human would attain each goal in a family of candidates were they pursuing it. We show where the two meet. From individual power, Fano’s inequality yields a floor $B(s)$, a strictly increasing function of individual power. This floor is a lower bound on what we term goal revelation, the mutual information $\mathbb{I}(G;\xi\mid s)$ between the human’s latent goal and the realised trajectory, or how much the interaction reveals about which goal was pursued. Empowerment caps revelation from above, through the directed information that the human’s realised behaviour generates from actions to trajectory, so that $B(s)\leq\mathbb{I}(G;\xi\mid s)\leq\mathbb{I}(\mathbf{A}_{h}\to\xi\mid s)\leq\mathfrak{E}_{h}(s)$. Each quantity can be large while the one below it stays at zero, highlighting the following failure modes. An assistant maximising empowerment can prefer an interface offering broad influence over goal-irrelevant degrees of freedom to one that lets the human attain every goal they might hold. An assistant maximising revelation cannot tell a working interface from one rewired so that every goal yields the wrong outcome, since relabelling goals leaves mutual information unchanged while zeroing every attainment probability. Positive guarantees therefore come only from the attainment end of the chain. A decomposition traces unrevealed goals to either distinct goals inducing the same behaviour or behaviour unreadable from outcomes; a satisfaction floor, computable from two statistics of interaction logs, offers a way to monitor the power users retain in a deployed system; and simulations in random environments show the three quantities correlated but far from interchangeable.

sections.body: The introduction motivates a formal power measure for AI safety, since optimal agents tend to acquire power and humans can be gradually disempowered. It reviews two measures: empowerment, the capacity in bits of the channel from an agent's actions to future states, and individual power, a goal-attainment measure built from counterfactual capabilities. It introduces goal revelation, the mutual information between the human's goal and the trajectory. The main result, Theorem 4.1, is a chain of bounds from individual power through revelation and directed information to empowerment. The authors state that none of the three quantities is by itself a safe objective.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: The paper links empowerment, goal revelation and individual power into one chain of bounds.

sections.body: The setup is a robot that aims to empower one human in a fully observable, discrete-time Markov game with a finite state space. Both agents act simultaneously, and the human's goal is drawn from a finite set of N candidates that the robot cannot observe. The human acts through a goal-conditioned policy, while the robot uses a state-conditioned Markov policy. Trajectories are generated over a finite window of T steps, with the goal fixed within each window. Information is measured in bits using base-2 logarithms.
sections.heading: Setup
sections.headline: The setup is a single-human, single-robot Markov game with a hidden goal chosen from a finite set.

sections.body: The section defines the three measures on a common trajectory space. Empowerment is the closed-loop directed-information capacity over the human's action sequences, bounded above by T log2 of the action-set size in bits per window. Capability is the expected discounted certificate time of a trajectory goal, computed by a truncated Bellman recursion, and the authors allow a discount of 1. Goals are trajectory properties, and first-outcome goals give pairwise disjoint satisfaction sets. Goal revelation is the mutual information between goal and trajectory under a reference prior, while individual power is scored with no prior.
sections.heading: Three Measures
sections.headline: Empowerment, capability and goal revelation are each defined on the same trajectory space with trajectory goals.

sections.body: The main theorem orders individual power, revelation, directed information and empowerment. Fano's inequality, applied to a decoder that guesses the goal from the goal the trajectory satisfies, gives the floor `B(s)`, which is clamped at zero. Massey's converse for channels with feedback gives the middle inequality, and the chain rule splits directed information into revelation plus a goal-blind term. Lemma 4.2 shows the floor is strictly increasing in individual power and reaches the ceiling log2 N. Remark 1 shows that deterministic pursuit has no goal-blind term. A decomposition splits the equivocation into goal-policy aliasing and policy-trajectory ambiguity.
sections.heading: The Bridge
sections.headline: Individual power gives a Fano floor on revelation, which is capped by directed information and empowerment.

sections.body: The section shows two failure modes. Proposition 2 builds environments where the toggle-board policy has 9 bits of empowerment and zero revelation. The assistance policy has 3.70 bits of empowerment and 2 bits of revelation, its ceiling, with every capability equal to 1. Proposition 3 relabels goals by a permutation, which leaves revelation unchanged while zeroing every capability. In the Table 2 example, revelation is 0.9 bits in both interfaces. The aligned interface has capability profile (0.9, 0.9) and floor 0.531 bits. The swapped interface has capabilities (0, 0) and floor 0.
sections.heading: Both Converses Fail
sections.headline: Capacity can be large while revelation is zero, and revelation can be large while attainment is zero.

sections.body: The section gives a second floor that needs no disjointness. It reads each trajectory only through whether it satisfies the pursued goal, using two statistics: efficacy, the probability that the pursued goal is satisfied within the window, and specificity, the expected number of goals a trajectory satisfies. Theorem 6.1 bounds revelation below by the binary relative entropy between efficacy and specificity over N. The limit cases give the ceiling when only the pursued goal is satisfied, and zero for goal-independent behaviour. Remark 2 shows the bound is the best achievable by a satisfaction-indicator decoder. The statistics are estimable from logs, but the bound depends on the labels and goal family and is a measurement, not a training signal.
sections.heading: A Floor for Overlapping Goal Families
sections.headline: A second floor, computed from two log statistics, bounds revelation for overlapping goal families.

sections.body: The canonical setting has N=5 outcomes, m=8 actions, alpha=1, and 1,000 environments of 50 states each. The ordering B(s) <= Rev(s) <= directed information <= empowerment holds on all 50,000 states. On average, empowerment is 0.585 bits, of which revelation is 0.497 bits (85.0%), of which the floor certifies 0.274 bits (54.6%). Mean within-environment Kendall tau is 0.751 for empowerment and revelation, 0.619 for revelation and the floor, and 0.581 for empowerment and the floor. Exact argmax agreement is 57.8% for empowerment and revelation and 41.8% for revelation and the floor. The authors note that this ensemble favours agreement by construction, since every outcome is a candidate goal.
sections.heading: Numerical Illustration
sections.headline: Across random bandit environments, the three scores are correlated but agree on the best state about half the time.

sections.body: The section sorts prior work by the pair of variables coupled, who holds the latent, and whether the quantity is maximised or minimised. Empowerment work includes Klyubin et al. and closed-loop forms, along with assistance proposals that substitute diversity of reachable states for capacity. Skill-discovery objectives maximise the same information with the agent's own latent, where relabelling is a symmetry. Intent-legibility and interface work either anchor to the true goal or, in the Reddy et al. case, note a one-step permutation invariance. Multi-agent and multi-human constructions are per-agent or goal-free, so the mechanisms of Section 5 cannot be expressed in them.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work differs from the chain in which variable holds the latent and whether the objective is maximised.

sections.body: The discussion states that maximising individual power maximises a guaranteed lower bound on revelation, which meets the ceiling where perfect capability is possible. It does not claim that maximising individual power maximises revelation in general. The design-time Fano floor uses counterfactual parameters, while the satisfaction floor is a deployment-time measurement, so it is a monitor rather than a training signal. The limitations are a finite window, full observability, and disjoint satisfaction sets for the Fano route. Information quantities depend on the reference prior and the candidate family. Capability requires modelling the human's policy, and one goal per window is assumed.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Maximising individual power guarantees a floor on revelation, but not revelation itself, so the satisfaction floor serves as a monitor.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the chain and states that positive guarantees come only from attainment. It lists four results: empowerment maximisation need not preserve attainment; revelation is capped by the behaviour ensemble's entropy; the satisfaction floor is a computable lower bound from two log statistics; and skill-discovery objectives inherit the invariance when pointed at a human's goals. It names three directions: a companion manuscript on goal-family gaming, relaxing full observability and finite windows, and bounding the error of the robot's model of the human. It makes no claim that any of the three measures is a safe objective on its own.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Only the attainment end of the chain gives positive guarantees about the power a human retains.

sections.body: The code for Section 7 and a script that recomputes the numbers quoted in this paper are available in a GitHub repository linked from the section text. The script lets readers check the reported values against the code. The section gives no further detail on dependencies or licence.
sections.heading: Code availability
sections.headline: Code for the Section 7 experiments and a number-recomputation script is available on GitHub.

sections.body: The disclosure states that Claude models and Gemini Pro 3.8 were used throughout the work. An extended exchange between one author and Claude developed the research questions and candidate results, and the author chose directions and retained results before drafting. Claude then drafted the text, carried out derivations, and wrote the code and tables, while the author steered revisions. The same author revised the prose for readability. Fresh Claude instances and Gemini red-teamed the mathematics, prose and claims, and checked cited works. The authors state that they take full responsibility for the paper.
sections.heading: Use of AI tools
sections.headline: The authors disclose using several large language models for ideation, drafting, code, tables and red-teaming.

sections.body: The appendix contains the proofs. For Theorem 4.1 it proves the feasibility upper bound, Massey's converse with a chain-rule identity, and the Fano lower bound through a satisfaction decoder. It proves Lemma 4.2 and gives a closed form for the floor. It proves Remark 1, Proposition 1, the Proposition 2 threshold, the Proposition 3 invariance and attainment claims, and Theorem 6.1 via data processing, and it gives Remark 2 via a softmax decoder. Parts of the Proposition 2 construction are not in the supplied text.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix gives proofs of Theorem 4.1, Lemma 4.2, Remark 1, Propositions 1 to 3 and Theorem 6.1.
